title: Present simple and continuous
tagline: Facts and routines against actions in progress, arrangements and things that annoy you.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 1 — multiple-choice cloze
Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations
Speaking Part 1 — talking about routines and life now
why: Both tenses look easy, but B2 First tests the edge cases: state verbs that never take -ing, present continuous for a fixed arrangement, and always + -ing for a complaint. Getting the choice wrong changes the meaning, not just the grammar.

diagrams.title: State verbs stay simple
diagrams.caption: Verbs of thought, feeling, senses and possession describe a state, not an action, so they don't take -ing — even when the meaning feels immediate.

head: Use
Present simple

Example
rows: subject + base verb (+s), with adverbs of frequency
Sofia checks her phone every ten minutes.
Liam is staying with his cousins this month.
We're meeting Miss Vega at four on Friday.
don't/doesn't + base verb / do/does + subject + base verb
Doesn't she live near the stadium? / Isn't he coming today?

examples.text: The 8:15 bus leaves from outside the market, not the main gate.
Miss Vega marks essays every weekend during term time.
Sofia doesn't eat meat, but she loves Andean cheese.
examples.note: a general fact + a state verb

use.point: Now, temporary situations and changing trends

examples.text: Look — Nadia is filming the rehearsal on her phone.
We're staying with my aunt in Cusco while our flat is being painted.
More schools are switching to digital textbooks every year.
Mateo is meeting the coach at six tomorrow to talk about the trip.
Liam is always forgetting his kit on training days.
We are performing at the festival on Saturday — it's already on the poster.

use.point: State verbs with an action meaning

examples.text: I think the second option is better, but we 're thinking about changing the topic anyway.
examples.note: think = opinion (simple) vs a mental process (continuous)

examples.text: This soup tastes amazing, but the chef is tasting it again before it goes out.
examples.note: taste = a sense (simple) vs an action (continuous)

watch_out.why: Know is a state verb — it never takes the continuous, whatever the time word suggests.

watch_out.wrong: She always is complaining about homework.
watch_out.why: Always goes after am/is/are, not before, in this pattern for complaints.

watch_out.wrong: The train leave at 6pm every day.
watch_out.why: Third person singular needs the -s ending in the present simple.

watch_out.wrong: We are meeting the coach every Tuesday for training.
watch_out.right: We meet the coach every Tuesday for training.
watch_out.why: A repeated routine takes the present simple, not the continuous — save meeting for one fixed occasion.
Have meaning possess is a state verb; only have meaning an action (having lunch, having a shower) can be continuous.

dialogue.title: What's on today?
dialogue.context: Sofia and Mateo are checking the sports and music schedule on the noticeboard while Liam keeps interrupting with excuses.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Wait, does the robotics club meet on Wednesdays or Thursdays this term?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Thursdays. And Miss Vega is running an extra session tomorrow because the regional contest is coming up.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Guys, I'm not joining today — my knee still hurts from Tuesday.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Since when do you care about your knee? You never warm up properly.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: I'm warming up right now, actually.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Sure you are. Anyway, the bus for the away match leaves at four sharp, not half past.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Nadia doesn't know that yet — she thinks it's at half four.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: She's always confusing the times. Someone should text her.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Good. And Liam, if your knee really hurts, tell the coach — don't just disappear.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Fine, fine. I promise I'll say something.

items.sentence: Look! Liam ___ his skateboard down the school ramp.
items.why: an action happening now (Look!) → present continuous

items.sentence: I ___ this song — can you turn it up?
items.why: love is a state verb; it doesn't take the continuous

items.sentence: We ___ a French exchange student next month — it's all arranged.
items.why: a fixed arrangement with a future time → present continuous

items.sentence: Nadia's always ___ her homework until the last minute.
items.why: always + be + verb-ing = an annoying repeated habit

items.sentence: The museum ___ at five on weekdays.
Right now, I ___ exactly what you mean.
items.why: see meaning understand is a state verb, even with right now

items.sentence: Every Saturday, Mateo and his dad ___ football in the park.

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with the correct form of the verb in brackets.

items.sentence: Miss Vega ___ (check) attendance at the start of every lesson.
Right now, the whole class ___ (wait) for the fire drill to finish.
Sofia ___ (not/like) horror films, but she watches them anyway for Liam.
We ___ (rehearse) the school play every day this week — the performance is on Friday.
___ (Liam/train) with the athletics team these days?
I ___ (not/understand) why the bus is leaving early today.
The shop on the corner ___ (not/open) on Sundays.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first. Use the word given. Do not change it. Use between two and five words.

items.second_end: his kit, and it really annoys Miss Vega.

items.second_end: with us for a few weeks while her flat is repaired.

The museum's doors close at five every weekday, without exception.

summary: Present simple: facts, routines and timetables — permanent and repeated.
Present continuous: now, temporary situations, fixed arrangements and complaints with always.
State verbs (know, want, believe, taste as a sense, have as possession) stay in the present simple, even when the time word suggests now.
Many verbs shift meaning between a state and an action — check which one the sentence needs.
In transformations, look for always, a fixed future arrangement or a finished routine to decide the tense.
